## 1. Direct answer

**It is not "best practice" in the full sense, but it is a recognised pattern and acceptable as a first stage, time-boxed and with guardrails.**

- **Recognised.** "One environment, two websites, a shared database and back-end" is a release channel, or "ring 0":
  - Fowler: blue-green that keeps one database and switches only the web layer (martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html).
  - Heroku: "an admin app running the same version of code, but with different configurations" (devcenter.heroku.com/articles/pipelines).
  - Microsoft: ring 0 and progressive exposure (learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/safe-deployments).
- **Not full best practice.** For software that holds customer accounts, the standard is to separate customer data from development, and from the agents that change things, before separating websites. Replit's fix after an agent deleted a production database was "Development and production databases are now automatically kept separate" (fortune.com/2025/07/23/ai-coding-tool-replit-wiped-database-called-it-a-catastrophic-failure/; docs.replit.com/features/data-and-storage/development-and-production). Railway's own guide puts the production boundary at a separate environment (railway.com/guides/isolate-staging-production).
- **What the choice protects.** It protects live users from bad website code, which is the largest single source of change: 90 edge-bff deploy sections in 30 days (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md, 2026-10-20 to 11-19).
- **What it does not protect.** The larger dangers to live accounts stay shared:
  - about 90 migrations in 30 days, about 15 of them on the edge_bff/terminal schemas;
  - 12 Postgres restarts;
  - out-of-memory kills at 512 MB and 1 GB (railway.ts:15-19);
  - 2 GB / 1 vCPU shared with backfills (railway.ts:20);
  - data crons and agent jobs using the owner login (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:1766; scripts/onboarding/run_job.sh:6-8);
  - no backup (PITR disabled, capacity_fairness_scale_cost.md:303; MU21 open, verification/edge_multiuser/AUDIT.md:891).
  Google SRE: "a bad canary can affect the control" when they share data stores (sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/).
- **As planned ("only the website is doubled"), it has concrete defects that must be fixed before EDGE_MULTIUSER goes on:**
  1. **The beta would swallow live users' sign-in codes.**
     - EDGE_EMAIL_ENABLED defaults to true and EDGE_EMAIL_MODE to log (config.py:124-125).
     - The sender claims any outbox row, with no site filter (mailer.py:84-86).
     - In log mode it marks the row sent and keeps the code readable (mailer.py:9-11).
  2. **Beta code would run live users' backtests.** The claim takes any owner's queued job (backtest.py:650-660). EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED switches the AI loop, the backtest loop and the email sender together (config.py:109; main.py:276-283). The hourly session clean-up lives inside the AI loop (worker.py:46-48).
  3. **Recent migrations would break an older live site.** Nothing guards "old code after a migration": store.ready guards only the reverse (edge-bff store.py:56-82). Examples:
     - 20261116_001: SET NOT NULL plus a new primary key on watchlist_items;
     - 20261117_002: DROP users_email_key;
     - 20261118_100: DROP subscriber_kind_check.
  4. **The workers change under the live page.** The page bundle carries its own copy of the screener and backtest cores (apps/edge-bff/Dockerfile:5-76). screener-worker deployed 23 times in 30 days, and backtest has no version check.
- **Verdict.** Accept it as Stage 1 for a closed launch with no paying users. Add the guardrails below, and commit now to a trigger for Stage 2, which moves account data off the market Postgres.
- **The judges.** Judge 1 preferred a separate production environment now (Design 2). Judge 2 preferred this guarded Stage 1 (Design 3). Summed scores: Design 3 108, Designs 1 and 2 101 each. Both judges call the user's choice acceptable only as a time-boxed first stage with guardrails.

## 2. Recommended architecture: "one environment, two release channels, guarded account data"
(Design 3, with grafts from Designs 1 and 2)

### 2.1 Topology
**Railway.** Project lucid-patience, environment `dev` only, not renamed, since the scripts use its ID (PROJECT_CONTEXT.md:9-12).

**edge-bff = the beta and admin console.**
- Keeps following `main` with Wait-for-CI (railway.ts:246-255).
- Address: edge-bff-dev.up.railway.app.
- New variables: `EDGE_SITE=beta` and `EDGE_EMAIL_ENABLED=false`.

**edge-bff-live (new).**
- Same Dockerfile, rootDirectory and start command as edge-bff.
- Source: `github("rednightt33/saniti", { branch: "live", checkSuites: true, rootDirectory: "/apps/edge-bff" })`, one replica, `--workers 1`.
  - Railway allows a trigger branch per service (docs.railway.com/guides/github-autodeploys).
  - One process is a code assumption (railway.ts:249; apps/edge-bff/README.md:576).
- Domain: the user's domain. Prefer a subdomain such as app.<domain>; an apex needs CNAME flattening or ALIAS from the DNS provider.
  - Railway needs a CNAME plus a TXT record. DNS can take up to 72 h. Behind Cloudflare, SSL must be "Full", not "Full (Strict)" (docs.railway.com/networking/domains/working-with-domains).
- Its own variables:
  - `EDGE_SITE=live`;
  - `EDGE_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=https://<domain>`. Only one origin is accepted (main.py:351), so www must redirect;
  - `EDGE_ENVIRONMENT` not dev/local;
  - `EDGE_EMAIL_MODE=resend`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EDGE_EMAIL_FROM`, `RESEND_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. config.py:135-138 refuses log mode only when EDGE_MULTIUSER is on outside dev/local.
- Values identical to edge-bff, as reference variables:
  - `EDGE_DATABASE_URL`: the code requires edge_bff_login (config.py:148-149). Two pools of 6 = 12 of the login's 20 connections (store.py:30; provision_edge_bff_login.py:71).
  - `EDGE_SESSION_SECRET`, `EDGE_MFA_KEY`, `EDGE_CODE_SECRET`, `TERMINAL_PROXY_KEY`, the worker keys, the Orc URL and key (see 2.5 for why the secrets stay identical).

**Shared, one copy each, as today:** Postgres, terminal-api, backtest-worker, screener-worker, the Orc stack, terminal-publisher, the terminal-display bucket, every cron, and the Telegram services.
- terminal-api accepts exactly one gateway key (terminal-api config.py:111,123; main.py:344-349). A per-site key would need a terminal-api code change, so it is not in this plan.

**Outside Railway:**
- The live origin goes into the terminal-display bucket CORS (scripts/terminal_bucket_cors.py; RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:6412). `set` replaces the whole list, so all three origins go in together.
- Resend's SPF/DKIM/DMARC records go on the domain, and its webhook points to the live domain at /api/v1/hooks/email/resend.
- Start DNS and Resend as soon as the domain is known.

### 2.2 Where each kind of data lives

| Data | Location | Written by | Guard |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accounts, identities, MFA, email codes, outbox, sessions, throttle, subscriptions, admin_audit | `edge_bff.*`, main Postgres | both sites; sessions tagged by `site` | nightly logical dump plus a dump before every APPLY; no ad hoc writes; expand-contract |
| Watchlists, layouts, drawings, presets, screener items | `edge_bff.*` | both sites | same |
| Backtest jobs, results, trials | `edge_bff.backtest_*` | the site that created the job (`site` column) | claims filtered by site |
| AI jobs and conversations | `edge_bff.jobs`, `public."AI_conversation*"` | beta only at launch (AI is admin-only, D1; CONTRACT.md:397) | in the dump |
| Terminal tiers, quotas, usage, access logs, owner rows | `terminal.*` | terminal-api (shared) | in the dump; expand-contract |
| Plan catalog rows (plans, plan_capabilities, overrides) | `edge_bff.*` | admin | they are live configuration; change only with the user's go |
| Market data | `public.*` → terminal-publisher → terminal-display bucket → terminal-api presigned URLs → both sites | data jobs, as today | one truth: a bad publication reaches both sites at once; existing reader checks; manual republish (AGENTS.md, Postgres memory step 4) |

- No page or worker calls terminal-api `/history`. A grep of apps/** .ts/.js for `history/price|broker` finds nothing (2026-11-19). So migrations on Price_Stock_Indonesia_IDX and Feature_05 are not live-facing in practice.
- Live personal data never goes into chat, logs or dev files. Diagnosis of user data uses counts only (graft from Design 2).

### 2.3 Site roles and loop owners (code change: per-loop switches replace the all-or-nothing EDGE_WORKER_ENABLED)

| Loop / feature | live | beta |
|---|---|---|
| Backtest loop | claims `site='live'` | claims `site='beta'` |
| AI job loop | off (no AI on live) | on |
| Email sender | on, the only Resend sender | off (`EDGE_EMAIL_ENABLED=false`) |
| Housekeeping: session, throttle and registration clean-up (store.py:354-358), backtest prune (backtest.py:749-752) | on, in its own maintenance task | off |
| Seeds | on | on (idempotent under advisory locks, accounts.py:102-109, :168-170) |

- One expand migration adds `site text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'beta'` on sessions, jobs and backtest_jobs.
  - The default must be 'beta', because every existing row is the admin's. Design 1's 'live' default was wrong.
  - From then on the code writes `site` explicitly, and adds an index on `(site, state, created_at)` for the claim.
- Each backtest answer gets a version stamp, as screener answers already carry (screener.py:5-10, :665-677).

### 2.4 Change flow

| Change | Beta | Live | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| edge-bff code | push `main`, CI-gated | only on "push ke live", same sha | `live` is always an ancestor of `main`; no cherry-picks; at most two versions alive (martinfowler.com/bliki/CanaryRelease.html); promote at least weekly |
| edge_bff / terminal migrations | applied once (shared DB) | same moment | expand only. A contract step (DROP, RENAME, SET NOT NULL, new PK/UNIQUE, ALTER TYPE, DROP CONSTRAINT) needs the header `-- contract-after-live: <sha>` with that sha an ancestor of `origin/live`. A lint in run_job.sh/migration_job.py and CI enforces it; it would have flagged all three examples in section 1. A fresh dump is required before APPLY (martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html; AWS blue-green whitepaper) |
| Data-table migrations and backfills | shared | shared | as today (large-update rules). Ad hoc heavy work outside IDX trading hours, because there is 1 vCPU (railway.ts:20) |
| terminal-api, backtest-worker, screener-worker | deploy as today | same instant | additive API only. Live smoke after every shared deploy; if it is red, roll that service back first. Escape hatch for an unavoidable break: a temporary `<name>-live` copy pinned to `live`. That needs the config.py hostname checks relaxed (config.py:166-182), about 0.25 day |
| Orc stack | as today | not used by live | becomes a shared service under the same rule when AI opens to users |
| Publisher output | SCHEMA_VERSION=1, additive only (publisher.py:158) | same | a breaking format publishes v2 beside v1 until `live` reads v2 |
| Plan catalog rows | shared rows | immediate | the user's go |

### 2.5 Promote, rollback and status (one script, `scripts/push_live.py`, in the owner's words)

**"push ke live" runs `--check`.**
1. Read the beta's `/version`, a new endpoint returning RAILWAY_GIT_COMMIT_SHA.
2. Require every check suite on that sha to be green, and a soak on the beta (default 24 h, adjustable).
3. Refuse, with the reason in plain Indonesian, when:
   - a check is red or pending;
   - beta's sha differs from the candidate;
   - a needed migration is not applied;
   - a user run is active (M340).
4. Show the commits since the current live tag, the pages that change, the migrations involved, and the beta smoke result.
5. Then ask for the go.

**`--apply`:**
1. Tag `live-YYYY-MM-DD-N` and fast-forward `live` (`git push origin <sha>:live`, fast-forward only).
2. Wait for edge-bff-live SUCCESS. SKIPPED is correct when apps/edge-bff did not change.
3. Read back `/ready` and `/version == sha`.
4. Run the live smoke with a synthetic free-plan account, whose password sits on a one-shot runner: sign in, BBCA in the Terminal, one Screener run, one small BBCA backtest, Overview/Radar/Watchlist reads.
5. Record the promote in RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md and send a Telegram notice.

**Wait-for-CI on `live`.** It works without workflow changes: backend-tests, backtest-lookahead and generated-files run `on: push` with no branch filter (verified). edge-bff-image and backtest-page-smoke are path-filtered.

**"balikin live" runs `--rollback`.**
- Within 120 h: Railway's rollback of the previous edge-bff-live deployment, which takes seconds (Pro image retention: docs.railway.com/reference/pricing/plans; railway.com/guides/roll-back-bad-deploy).
- After 120 h: move `live` back to the previous tag (`--force-with-lease`) and redeploy, or CLI-upload a `git archive` of that tag.
- Then the smoke test.
- Never a database step, because migrations are expand-only.

**"status live" runs `--status`:** the live tag, its date, and what is on beta but not yet on live.

**A GitHub ruleset on `live`** blocks accidental pushes. Rulesets are available: the repository is public (`gh api repos/rednightt33/saniti`: visibility public). But the agents' GitHub credential has admin:true, so the ruleset guards only by convention.

**Secrets stay identical on both sites.**
- A separate EDGE_SESSION_SECRET isolates nothing. Sessions are looked up by plain sha256 (security.py:42-43). The secret only signs CSRF (security.py:46-47) and keys the sign-in throttle HMAC (throttle.py:61-63; main.py:235), so separate secrets would double the attempts an attacker gets on the admin account.
- EDGE_MFA_KEY derives the TOTP secret (auth_flows.py:538-577). EDGE_CODE_SECRET hashes email codes (auth_flows.py:127).
- Isolation comes from three things: host-only cookies with no Domain attribute (auth_flows.py:405-407), the `sessions.site` check, and the separate hosts.

### 2.6 How admin features stay off the public site
- **Beta (`EDGE_SITE=beta`):**
  - every request needs an admin principal (admin_owners, config.py:120) with MFA, or gets 403, enforced on the server;
  - registration, forgot and reset are refused, with wording that points to the live domain (edge-labels.js);
  - a "BETA · <sha>" banner;
  - AI Monitor, lab chunks (`/{app}-app/lab/{name}`, CONTRACT.md:270-271), the Phase 4 /admin page and `/api/v1/admin/*` live only here.
- **Live (`EDGE_SITE=live`):** a site mask strips `admin.access`, `monitor.*` and every lab-stage capability from every principal. The /admin, Monitor, lab and AI routes answer 404. The admin can sign in on live and sees it as a customer does.
- **Why this layout:** NIST SP 800-53 SC-2 separates management from user functions, including "isolating administrative interfaces on different domains" (csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/sc/sc-2/). OWASP: "not to mix web applications of different security levels on the same domain" (cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).
- **Optional, about 0.1 day:** rename the session cookie to the `__Host-` prefix before switch-on, when only the admin would be signed out once (same OWASP page). Later, Cloudflare Access or an IP allowlist could go in front of the beta.

### 2.7 Cost per month (Railway Pro; memory USD 10/GB-month, volume 0.15, bucket 0.015; railway.com/pricing)
**Today:** USD 33.43 of usage, measured 2026-10-24..28 (capacity_fairness_scale_cost.md:50, table :96-110). The November pace is about USD 40 (USD 29.71 used by 11-13 in a period that began 10-21; ERRORS M424). Pro includes USD 20, so the bill is about the usage.

| Added | Basis | USD/month |
|---|---|---|
| edge-bff-live | edge-bff measured at 0.082 GB = 1.00 (capacity doc :105); more with users | 1-1.5 |
| Logical dump cron and private bucket | schema size not measured, expected under 1 GB | < 0.3 |
| Moving the restart times, option (a) in section 5 | at most about 1.7 GB of cache × extra hours × USD 0.0139/GB-h | 0-3 |
| Native volume backups or PITR (optional, decision 6) | not measured; copy-on-write keeps changed blocks, and backfills rewrite the 53 GB database often (docs.railway.com/reference/backups) | 1-5 or more; read back after a week |
| **Total** | | **about 1.5-2 core; about 3-10 with the options**, so about USD 36-50 of usage |

Not included: the domain and Resend (free-tier limits not checked).

| # | Work | Days |

| a | Usage-limit headroom and soft warning (the user, in the dashboard); restart times moved with scripts/set_postgres_restart_times.py | 0.2 |
| b | `EDGE_SITE`: beta admin gate, registration refused on beta, live site mask and 404s, `sessions.site` binding, banner, `/version`, tests | 1.5-2 |

| d | edge-bff-live in railway.ts, domain/TLS, Resend DNS and webhook, CORS; restart_postgres.py checks /ready of both sites (today only edge-bff, restart_postgres.py:314-327); M340 covers both | 1 |
| e | push_live.py (check/apply/rollback/status), live smoke runner, ruleset | 1.5 |

- The user's own time is about 1 h: DNS records, Resend domain verification, the usage limit, and keys entered in the dashboard.
- Order: a, c, b and f must land before EDGE_MULTIUSER is switched on, even before the live domain exists. d and e come before the domain opens. g may slip to week 1, but its rule goes into AGENTS.md on day 1.
- Timeline: with a go by about 21 Nov, 3 Dec is realistic and 26 Nov is tight. The remaining EXEC-MU-ACCOUNTS work competes for the same days; 20261118_001/_002/_100 are still pending.
- **After launch:**
  - a compat-live CI job: replay the edge_bff/terminal migrations on a throwaway Postgres and run the live tag's DB tests against the candidate schema (Design 2), about 1 day;
  - a "status live" Telegram button;
  - an external uptime ping (telegram-monitor sleeps).

**New AGENTS.md section "Beta and live":**
1. `live` moves only through push_live.py, after the user's "push ke live" and go.
2. Never claim a live change before edge-bff-live is at SUCCESS and the sha has been read back.
3. Expand-contract for edge_bff, terminal, AI_conversation* and publisher formats, with the contract header.
4. Every shared deploy keeps working with the live sha and ends with the live smoke.
5. No ad hoc writes to the user schemas; a dump before any APPLY on them; aggregates only for user data.
6. Plan catalog rows change only with the user's go.
7. Email and housekeeping run only on live; the beta stays admin-only.
8. M340 and the Postgres restart cover both sites; ad hoc heavy work runs outside trading hours.

### 2.9 Risks this does not cover
1. **One Postgres, 2 GB / 1 vCPU.** A heavy job, an out-of-memory kill or a planned restart (about 12 s) stops sign-in and the Terminal on both sites.
2. **Owner-level reach.**
   - Data crons and runners use `${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}`.
   - The daily GitHub workflow builds an owner URL through the public TCP proxy (database-schema-docs.yml:99-106; proxy at railway.ts:10).
   - Grants cannot stop the owner, so only rules and backups protect user rows.
3. **Agents' credentials reach live.**
   - Railway: the agents use the proxy's account credential (ERRORS_AND_SOLUTIONS.md:7754-7756). Environment RBAC is Enterprise-only (docs.railway.com/reference/environments).
   - GitHub: the agents' credential is repo admin.
4. **Shared terminal-api, workers and publisher output change under live.** The smoke detects a break; nothing blocks it.
5. **Page/worker skew.** The Screener tolerates it partly (versions and needs_review, screener.py:454-455, :697). The backtest has only the new stamp.
6. **The beta's newest code manages live users through /admin.** Every action is audited in admin_audit, but it is still the untested version.
7. **Market-data errors reach both sites at the same publish.**
8. **Workspace-wide stops.** M424: hard limit 30 against 29.71 used, soft limit 0, every service down for about 20 h (ERRORS_AND_SOLUTIONS.md:7590-7608); also M346. No environment layout avoids this; only headroom and a warning help.
9. **The repository is public**, so code, migrations, railway.ts and runbooks are world-readable while the account database has a public proxy (password-protected).

## 3. Alternatives the user could prefer
- **A. Light production environment now (Design 2, Judge 1's pick).**
  - What it is: a new empty `production` environment with edge-bff, an edge-admin host, terminal-api, both workers, a small Postgres with PITR and no proxy, and its own bucket. It is fed only by a `market-release` copier of the published files. Promotion goes through GitHub-approved workflows. The agents get a dev-scoped project token ("can only be used to authenticate requests to that environment", docs.railway.com/integrations/api).
  - Trade-off: live accounts are fully off the dev Postgres and out of the agents' reach. It costs about +USD 10-18 a month (the screener's awake memory is about 1.15 GB, not 0.4-0.7) and about 7 agent-days plus about 2 h of the user's time; 3 Dec is at risk; it reverses the user's 2026-11-19 choice.
  - It is real only if the agents also get a non-admin GitHub identity. A project token also breaks serviceConnect (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:1767) and today's runbooks that use the account credential.
- **B. Pin the workers from day one (Design 1).**
  - What it is: add screener-worker-live (following `live`) and backtest-worker-live (CLI upload of the live sha in each promote).
  - Trade-off: it removes page/worker skew, for about +USD 3-8 a month, +1 day (the config.py hostname change), and one more upload step per promote.
- **Not recommended: the choice as-is, without guardrails.** It is cheapest (+USD 1-1.5), but it carries the defects in section 1 (swallowed codes, beta code running live jobs, broken old site after a migration).

## 4. Growth path (the trigger for each next step)
1. **Pinned live worker copies.** When: a breaking core change is pending, or the first page/worker skew incident. Effort and cost: 1 day, +USD 3-8.
2. **Stage 2: account data on its own small Postgres.**
   - What: edge_bff and the terminal account tables, with PITR and no TCP proxy. Only the edge-bff, edge-bff-live and terminal-api logins write; agents read aggregates; migrations need the user's go. Data crons and runners move off the owner URL to a role with no rights on edge_bff/terminal.
   - When, whichever comes first: the first paying user or the payment adapter going live (CONTRACT.md section 11); about 50 registered users; the first incident where a data job, a restart or an agent touched user data or stopped sign-in.
   - Effort and cost: 3-4 days (terminal-api needs a second database connection, store.py:12-16), +USD 2-5.
3. **AI opened to a paid plan (D1 changes).** Orc becomes live-facing: either a live copy following `live`, or the two-version rule plus smoke. AI_conversation* then holds customer data and joins Stage 2's database.
4. **Stage 3: a separate Railway production environment (Alternative A).**
   - When: a second operator joins; UU PDP or payment compliance requires it; shared-service changes break live more than about twice a month; or Stage 2 is not enough.
   - Preconditions: agents on a dev-scoped project token, a GitHub identity without admin, and a check of read-only bucket keys.
   - Effort and cost: 1-2 weeks, +USD 10-18.
5. **A separate workspace for production.** When: a workspace-wide stop hits live users after launch.
6. **A full copy of dev.** Not justified at any foreseeable team size: it roughly doubles the bill and every data operation.

## 5. Decisions the user must take (each needs its context first, per AGENTS.md)
1. **Stage 1 shape:** (a) the user's choice plus the guardrails above [recommended]; (b) a light production environment now (Alternative A).
2. **Beta sign-in:** (a) admin only, as decided; (b) admin plus named test-* accounts, so registration and plan gates can be tested on the beta before a push.
3. **Workers:** (a) shared, with an escape hatch [recommended]; (b) pinned from day one, +USD 3-8, +1 day.
4. **Postgres restart times** (today 09:45 and 20:45 WIB, railway.ts:295; 09:45 is in trading hours):
   - (a) about 12:15 (lunch break) and 23:45 WIB, about +USD 0-3;
   - (b) drop the morning restart and keep 23:45, about +USD 5-10;
   - (c) keep the current times.
   The script refuses times near other crons or in B6.
5. **Usage limit:** a new hard limit (suggestion: about 2× the expected bill, about USD 80) and a soft warning (about USD 50).
6. **Backups:** (a) a logical dump of user data only, cents a month [minimum]; (b) the dump plus native volume backups or PITR, cost not measured.
7. **Public TCP proxy on the main Postgres:** (a) keep it, but move the daily schema-docs workflow to a read-only login; (b) close it and run that job inside Railway.
8. **Repository visibility:** keep it public, or make it private. Private hides the code and runbooks, but may cost Actions minutes and ruleset or environment features (to verify).
9. **Promote rules:** a 24 h soak on beta (yes or no), and whether the agent may roll live back by itself when the post-promote smoke fails, reporting at once.
10. **The Stage 2 trigger** to commit to now: the first paying user, about 50 users, or the first incident.
11. **Domain form:** a subdomain (app.<domain>) or the apex. This depends on whether the DNS provider supports CNAME flattening.

## 6. Claims dropped or corrected (do not repeat these)

judged.verdict_on_user_choice:
Yes, the choice is acceptable as Stage 1. One environment with two edge-bff sites on a shared database is a recognised pattern: a permanent ring-0/admin channel, blue-green with a shared database, or Heroku's admin app at the same stage. Website code is most of the change volume (90 of the deploy sections in 30 days). For this owner it is the right cost and time trade-off: about +1-1.5 USD a month for the site itself, against +9-18 USD and a riskier launch date for a separate production environment.

It is not safe as described ("only the website is doubled"), because the code shares background work and side effects between the sites. Before EDGE_MULTIUSER is switched on, add:

(1) **Pin live.** edge-bff-live follows branch `live`. Only push_live.py moves it, on the user's "push ke live", after a check, with tags and rollback ("balikin live"). The sha is read back from /version, and a GitHub ruleset on `live` blocks other pushes.

(2) **Site roles in code (EDGE_SITE).**
- The beta is admin-only on every request, server-side, with registration refused.
- Live has no admin, lab, Monitor or AI surfaces.
- A `site` column, defaulting to 'beta' for existing rows, goes on sessions, jobs and backtest_jobs, and claims filter on it.
- Email and housekeeping (session, throttle and registration clean-up, backtest prune) run only on live.
- Set EDGE_EMAIL_ENABLED=false on beta. Without it, beta's log-mode sender claims live users' code emails and marks them sent without sending (config.py:124-125, mailer.py:9-11).

(3) **Same secrets on both sites.** EDGE_SESSION_SECRET, EDGE_MFA_KEY and EDGE_CODE_SECRET are identical. Separate secrets do not isolate sessions (sessions are a plain sha256, security.py:42-43). They would split the throttle and break the admin's authenticator on one site.

(4) **Protect user data.**
- A nightly logical dump of edge_bff, terminal and AI_conversation*, plus one before any APPLY that touches them, and one restore drill. No backup exists today (MU21 open, PITR disabled).
- A contract-migration lint (`contract-after-live`). The recent 20261116_001, 20261117_002 and 20261118_100 would have broken an older live site.
- No ad hoc writes to user schemas.

**Live user data lives only in the production Postgres.**

**Market data is produced once, in dev, as today.** It reaches live only as files:
1. dev jobs write dev Postgres;
2. terminal-publisher writes dev `terminal-display` (cron `0,30 0,1,12 * * *` UTC);
3. `market-release` in production polls dev's state.json (cron about every 30 minutes, 07:15-09:15 and 19:15-20:15 WIB; a run with no new state.json does nothing). It reads only the dev bucket, over public S3 with dev's bucket key held in production, and never touches dev's Postgres, so it adds no load there.
4. It copies only the new content-addressed objects to the live bucket, in the publisher's own order: data files, then manifests, then state.json (publisher.py:122-125).
5. It deletes old objects with the M250 delay rule (600 s after state.json; publisher.py:536-537, :574-575). It keeps the objects of the last 3 promoted publications, so live can be pinned back.

**How a bad data job is kept from live**
- A wrong migration, backfill, cron or out-of-memory event in dev cannot touch live users' data: different database, different network, different credentials.
- Bad or broken publications are held. Live keeps the last good one, and Telegram says "data per <date>, held because …". The hold checks:
  - **Structure:** every file a manifest names exists, and its sha256 and bytes match.
  - **Format:** `SCHEMA_VERSION` (publisher.py:158) is one that live terminal-api reports it reads, from a new `/compat` route.
  - **Regression:** `data_through` never goes backwards; ticker or row counts per dataset never drop more than 1%; the Radar, Overview and Watchlist indexes are present.
  - **Rewrites:** history of older years rewritten for more than 20 tickers in one run is held. Fewer is promoted and listed (splits and rights, UPDATE_TABLE.md part C).
  - The thresholds sit in one named table, like FASTLANE_DEFAULTS.
  - "Promote held data anyway" is a production workflow that the user approves in GitHub.
- At launch run the hold in report-only mode for one week, then enforce it.
- What it does not catch: plausible but wrong numbers (section 7).

## 3. Change flow
Each kind of change, from beta to live:
- **Website code (edge-bff):** push to main deploys the beta as today (checkSuites, railway.ts:247). Live gets it only through "push ke live".
- **Worker code and terminal-api:** they reach dev as today. Live gets them in the same promotion, from the same commit, so in live the page bundle and the worker cores always match. Today there is no handshake between them.
- **AI (Orc, governors, sandbox):** dev only. There is no live path until AI opens to users (section 7).
- **Data-table migrations (public.*, the catalogs; about 64 of the 90 in the last 30 days):** dev only, never live.
- **User-schema migrations (`edge_bff` and `terminal`; 23 files today):**
  - applied on dev first, as today;
  - in CI: replayed from zero on a throwaway Postgres;
  - in CI: the compat-live test runs the current live tag's database tests against the candidate schema. Nothing guards "old code after the migration" today (store.py:56-82 guards only the reverse).
  - applied on live by `live-migrator` at promotion.
  - Expand first, contract only in a later promotion, once compat-live shows no live reader is left. Each file declares `-- phase: expand|contract`.
  - live-migrator keeps its own ledger in the live database. APPLIED.sha256 stays dev's.
- **Publisher output:** automatic through market-release (section 2). A format change writes the new SCHEMA_VERSION beside the old one until live reads the new one.

**"Push ke live", in the owner's words**
1. The user says "push ke live" in chat.
2. The agent starts workflow `promote-live` for the commit running on the beta. The commit must be green on every suite and have run on the beta for at least 24 hours (default, adjustable).
3. GitHub asks the user to approve. One tap in the GitHub app ("Approve deployment"), with "prevent self-review" on.
4. The workflow then:
   1. writes a pg_dump of the live database to `live-backups` (seconds: the database is small);
   2. runs `live-migrator` (expand migrations only);
   3. deploys with `railway up` from the exact commit tree, waiting for SUCCESS and /ready at each step, in this order: terminal-api, then backtest-worker, then screener-worker, then edge-bff, then edge-admin. Services whose paths did not change are skipped.
   4. smoke-tests the domain;
   5. tags `live-YYYYMMDD-n`, fast-forwards branch `live`, and reports to Telegram.
- CLI upload is required anyway: "serviceConnect to GitHub is refused for the project token" (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:1767). It also gives a fixed deploy order, which autodeploy from a branch does not.
- A ruleset on `live` with an empty bypass list means no agent can move `live` by hand.

**Rollback** ("balikin live")
- Workflow `rollback-live`, approved the same way, puts the previous tag back in the same order.
- Within 120 hours it uses Railway's image rollback, which takes seconds (Pro image retention). After that it rebuilds from the tag, which takes minutes.
- The database is not rolled back: expand-only means the previous code still works.
- For data damage: restore the pre-promotion dump or PITR into a new Postgres in production, then cut over. Railway's PITR restore creates a new service (docs.railway.com/volumes/point-in-time-recovery).
- Market data: `market-release pin <previous>`.

## 7. Risks, what it does not protect against, and the growth path

**What it does not protect against**
1. **Workspace-wide stops.** The usage limit stopped every service three times in November (RAILWAY_CHANGELOG.md:1316, :663-675, :513). An sfo outage, account compromise or billing failure would also stop live.
   - Now: set the usage limit well above the expected bill and alert at 75%.
   - Later: a separate workspace for production.
2. **If the agents keep the account credential,** the Railway separation holds by convention only. An agent could deploy into production. The switch to a dev project token is a precondition. Verify that the CLI tasks agents run (service create, variables, Run Now, logs) work with it; `railway usage` already fails with a project token.
3. **If the agents' GitHub identity is the user's own account,** it could approve deployments or edit rulesets, and the promote gate becomes soft. Verify which identity the agents push with.
4. **Beta coverage is thin.** The beta has one user, so multi-user paths see little real traffic before live. Run golden multi-user tests with test-* accounts on the beta, smoke-test after each promotion, and keep rollback fast.
5. **Plausible but wrong market data passes the checks** and reaches live. Value-level checks stay dev's job, as today.
6. **A hold makes live data one session stale.** It shows to users as "data per <date>".
7. **Config can drift between environments.** Railway itself warns that isolation creates drift. Keep one railway.ts with `ctx.environment`, and run `config plan` inside promote-live.
8. **Live Postgres is a single instance with no HA.** A crash means downtime; a restore takes minutes to hours.
9. **edge-admin holds full access to user data.** MFA, the audit trail and the separate host reduce this but do not remove it.
10. **market-release holds dev's full bucket key,** because read-only bucket keys are not verified. A bug there could damage dev's bucket, never live's.
11. **UU PDP 27/2022 duties are not researched.**

**Growth path**
- **Stage 2, a separate workspace for production** (its own usage limit and billing, plus an external uptime monitor and a status page). When: the first paying user, about 50 active users, or the first live outage caused by the workspace.
- **Stage 3, AI for users.** When: AI opens to non-admin users (D1 changes). Either:
  - (a) run Orc and the governors in production on a read-only market copy;
  - (b) keep AI in dev and expose one narrow, keyed public API.
  - The user decides then. Until then AI stays in dev.
- **Stage 4, a staging environment plus PR environments for edge-bff.** When: the team or compliance grows. The staging database can be an anonymised copy of the live database, which is small.

  5. **Page/worker version skew.** It is partly tolerated by the Screener's versions (see above); the backtest has no check.
  6. **Market-data errors reach both sites at once**, by design.
  7. **The beta's newest code works on real data** through the admin dashboard.

# Research report: separating the admin/beta site from live production (EDGE, 2026-11-19)

## 0. Short answer
- **Yes, the pattern is recognised.** "One environment, two websites, a shared database and shared back-end" has known names. Fowler describes it as a blue-green variation that keeps one database and switches only the web and domain layers. In ring terms it is a permanent "ring 0" or internal-beta channel. It is not the standard full staging/production split. The sources accept it when four conditions hold:
  1. schema changes are expand-contract, so both versions work against one schema;
  2. the shared services stay compatible with both website versions;
  3. side effects and background jobs have exactly one owner;
  4. the live site can be rolled back independently.
- **The main gap.** The chosen design isolates only the web UI. Everything that can hurt live users is still shared and still changes directly:
  - AI agents applying SQL and migrations to the one Postgres;
  - shared services that auto-deploy from `main`;
  - heavy data jobs and planned Postgres restarts on the same 2 GB Postgres that will hold customer accounts.
- **What industry practice says.** It isolates customer and production data from development first; the web tier comes second. This is the main finding to put in front of the user.
- **Recommendation for a solo, cost-sensitive, AI-operated owner.** Keep the user's choice for launch, with the guardrails in section 7. The next step, when there are real users or payments, is to move only the account, session, subscription and job data (`edge_bff`) to its own small Postgres. Market data is still made once and shared read-only. A full copy of production is not justified at this stage.

## 1. Is "one environment, two website versions, a shared production database and shared back-end" accepted?

**Names for it**
- **Blue-green with a shared database.** Fowler: a variation is to "use the same database, making the blue-green switches for web and domain layers" (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). AWS's blue-green whitepaper: "a general recommendation is to decouple schema changes from the code changes. This way, the relational database is outside of the environment boundary … and shared between the blue and green environments" (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/blue-green-deployments/best-practices-for-managing-data-synchronization-and-schema-changes.html).
- **Canary release / internal users first.** Fowler: canaries can go to "internal employees first" (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CanaryRelease.html). Google SRE: a canary is "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation" (https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/). The beta differs in one way: it is not time-limited. It is a permanent channel.
- **Ring deployment.** Microsoft puts the service's own development team in Ring 0 and widens to larger groups only after health checks pass. The Azure Well-Architected Framework calls this "progressive exposure" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/implement-test-progressive-exposure-deployment/3-explore-ci-cd-deployment-rings, https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/operational-excellence/safe-deployments).
- **Same code, two apps with different config at one stage.** Heroku Pipelines: "the production stage might have the main production app and an admin app running the same version of code, but with different configurations" (https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/pipelines). This is close to beta=admin and live=public.
- **Not a dark launch.** Fowler defines dark launching as running new back-end behaviour for existing users without showing it. That is a different technique (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/DarkLaunching.html).

**Known risks**
- **Shared state lets the beta harm live.** SRE: "the canary population and the control may share backends, frontends, networks, data stores … a bad canary can affect the control"; also "Traffic teeing also doesn't adequately identify risk in stateful systems" (https://sre.google/workbook/canarying-releases/).
- **Schema is the hard part.** Fowler: databases "can often be a challenge with this technique". The schema must "support both the new and old version" (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/BlueGreenDeployment.html). AWS: deletive changes carry "increased risk … failures in the schema modification process can impact your production environment" (AWS whitepaper above).
- **Two versions to maintain.** Fowler: "you have to manage multiple versions of your software at once … keep the number of concurrent versions to a minimum" (CanaryRelease above).
- **Beta writes and side effects reach production.** Railway's own canary guide warns that canaries copying production variables can write to production data. It advises using `RAILWAY_ENVIRONMENT_NAME` to turn off emails, payments and webhooks in canaries (https://railway.com/guides/ship-on-merge-pr-canaries).
- **Data loss caused by agents is the worst failure here.** In the July 2025 Replit case, an AI agent deleted a live production database during a code freeze. Replit's response was "Development and production databases are now automatically kept separate" (https://fortune.com/2025/07/23/ai-coding-tool-replit-wiped-database-called-it-a-catastrophic-failure/). Replit's docs now say "Agent is not able to modify the production database" and give it read-only access through a replica (https://docs.replit.com/features/data-and-storage/development-and-production).

**When the sources consider it acceptable**
- All schema changes are backward compatible: expand before the code change, contract after it (AWS, Fowler).
- Releases are small and frequent, gated by tests and health checks. Rollback is fast (Azure SDP above; Railway guide above).
- Canary writes and side effects are controlled (Railway guide).

What the sources do not support: the change channel for the shared parts (database, back-end services) bypassing the beta. In EDGE today it does bypass it. See section 7.

## 2. The standard alternatives (pros, cons, cost for a small team)

Railway prices (https://railway.com/pricing):
- memory about $10 per GB-month;
- vCPU about $20 per vCPU-month;
- volume $0.15 per GB-month;
- egress $0.05 per GB;
- Hobby $5/month including $5 of usage, Pro $20/month including $20.

| Option | Pros | Cons | Cost for EDGE (estimate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Separate staging and production, each with its own database** (Railway "Duplicate environment"; Heroku pipeline of apps) | Strongest isolation. Railway: "an isolated instance of every service", each environment has its own private network ("There is no route between the two networks"), own bucket ("Staging code cannot delete production objects"), and "Sync copies configuration, not data" (https://railway.com/guides/isolate-staging-production). Heroku: promotion copies the tested build unchanged (https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/pipelines). AWS: production and non-production in separate accounts as the strongest boundary (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/organizing-your-aws-environment/benefits-of-using-multiple-aws-accounts.html). | "Isolation creates drift risk" (Railway guide). Market data would have to be made twice or copied. Sealed variables must be set again. Environment RBAC is Enterprise-only, so it adds no access separation on Hobby or Pro (Railway guide). Every operation the AI agents run becomes two. | Roughly doubles the always-on services, the data jobs and the 2 GB Postgres (up to about $20/month of memory alone), plus about $3.5/month for a 23 GB volume copy. Not recommended now. |
| **B. Staging with a copy or anonymised snapshot of production data** | Realistic tests. Fowler and Sadalage list "a tool to anonymize production data for development use" (https://martinfowler.com/articles/evodb.html). Neon branches are a "copy-on-write clone" that does not load the parent, and "schema-only branching" is available for sensitive data (https://neon.com/docs/introduction/branching). | Personal data copied into lower environments is a privacy and security risk. Pseudonymised data is still personal data under GDPR-style law (secondary: https://sprintlaw.co.uk/articles/ico-anonymisation-guidance-how-uk-businesses-can-anonymise-data-under-gdpr/). Indonesian law (UU PDP 27/2022) was not researched and should be checked before copying account data. Railway Postgres has no copy-on-write branching. A 23 GB copy is a large update under AGENTS.md (page cache and restart). | High one-off memory and IO per refresh. Market data is not personal, so copying it is a cost issue, not a privacy issue. |
| **C. Read-only sharing of reference/market data between environments** | Produce once, read everywhere. PostgreSQL logical replication covers "sharing a subset of the database between multiple databases" and "giving access to replicated data to different groups of users" (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/logical-replication.html). AWS: object stores are "often easier to share between the two environments" than relational stores (AWS whitepaper). | Railway buckets are per environment with their own credentials. Cross-environment access goes over the public network (Railway guide; EXEC.md:15983-15985). Whether Railway buckets can issue read-only credentials was NOT verified. Logical replication across Railway environments needs a public TCP proxy and wal_level=logical (not verified on this Postgres). | Low. This fits EDGE's existing architecture (section 3). |
| **D. Feature flags in one deployment** | No second site. Fowler: permissioning toggles gate beta features "to internal and beta users", decided per request. Release toggles are cheap (https://martinfowler.com/articles/feature-toggles.html). Azure SDP recommends flags for exposure and fast rollback (Azure page above). | Flags carry a "carrying cost". Release toggles "should generally not stick around much longer than a week or two", and the off and on paths both need tests (Fowler). A crash in shared code still reaches everyone. A flag does not protect against a bad deploy, only against a bad feature. | Zero infrastructure. EDGE already does this (`EDGE_MULTIUSER`, the plan tiers). |
| **E. Preview environment per pull request** | A disposable copy per change. Railway: "The PR environment is the canary", deleted on merge, and "Focused PR environments" deploy only the services that changed (https://railway.com/guides/ship-on-merge-pr-canaries). | They start with empty databases or minimal seed data (https://docs.railway.com/guides/preview-deployments-with-pr-environments). They copy production variables, including the database URL, unless overridden (canary guide). Render needs a Pro plan and does not copy data (https://render.com/docs/preview-environments). EDGE's agents push to `main` directly, without pull requests. | Pay per second while open. It could be added later for edge-bff only. |

## 3. Data produced once (daily market jobs) but needed by both staging and production
The common practice is to treat such data as a published, read-only product that both environments consume. It is not copied into each environment's own database.
- In blue-green, the shared data store sits outside the environment boundary (AWS whitepaper, Fowler).
- Object storage is the easiest to share (AWS).
- Publish/subscribe replication of a subset, read by other databases, is a built-in Postgres use case (PostgreSQL docs above).
- The Twelve-Factor rule is about parity of backing service type and version across environments, not about duplicating data: "All deploys of the app … should be using the same type and version of each of the backing services" (https://12factor.net/dev-prod-parity).

EDGE fact: the user-facing services already read market data only through terminal-api, from files that terminal-publisher writes to the bucket (EXEC.md:15988-15990; `.railway/railway.ts` terminal-api env with `TERMINAL_BUCKET_*` and its own `terminal` schema, lines 191-196). That "published files" boundary is where a future production environment would attach. Data jobs and the 23 GB market Postgres stay in one place, and production reads the published files read-only. This is option 2, "light production", from EXEC.md:15993-15994, and it matches the guidance.

## 4. Admin interface: the same app with roles, or a separate deployment and host?
- **Separate management from user functions.** NIST SP 800-53 SC-2: "Separate user functionality … from system management functionality". It can be physical or logical, including "isolating administrative interfaces on different domains and with additional access controls" (https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/sc/sc-2/).
- **OWASP Developer Guide (Administrative Interfaces; read only via mirrors):** high-value systems should put admin functions on separate hosts, reachable only through management networks (https://sqwrl.gitbooks.io/owasp-developer-guide/content/04-OperationalSecurity/Administrative-Interfaces.html). Practitioner caveat: network restriction does not replace application authentication (https://www.indusface.com/blog/admin-console-protection/).
- **MFA on admin interfaces.** ASVS 4.x 4.3.1: "Verify administrative interfaces use appropriate multi-factor authentication" (mirror: https://owasp-aasvs4.readthedocs.io/en/latest/V4.3.html).
- **Cookies and hosts.** OWASP Session Management: do not set the `Domain` attribute. Use the `__Host-` prefix for session IDs. "It is recommended not to mix web applications of different security levels on the same domain". A role change to administrator requires a new session ID. Re-authenticate after high-risk events (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html).
- **Separate app, same code, different config is normal.** Heroku Pipelines explicitly allows a production admin app beside the public app (pipelines page above).

What this means for EDGE:
- The beta on `*.up.railway.app` (admin only) and the live site on the user's domain are different sites. Cookies are naturally separate if neither sets `Domain`.
- Use `__Host-` session cookies on both.
- Give each site its own `EDGE_SESSION_SECRET`, so a session from one site is never valid on the other.
- Keep MFA for admin (`EDGE_MFA_KEY` already exists).
- The live site should not serve admin-only tools at all, or should demand admin plus re-authentication.
- Enforce "admin only" on the beta server-side, at sign-in and on every request. Hiding the link is not enough.

## 5. Database migrations while two versions run at once, and rollback
- **Expand, migrate, contract.** Fowler ParallelChange: "In the expand phase you augment the interface to support both the old and the new versions … migrate … contract phase to remove the old version". If the contract step never happens, "the codebase can end up worse" (https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ParallelChange.html).
- **AWS:** schema changes come first and are additive, and the old version must tolerate extra columns ("ignore fields it can't map"). Deletive changes come only after the old version is gone (AWS whitepaper).
- **Prisma's seven steps:** add the new structure (nullable or with defaults), dual-write, backfill, test, switch reads, stop writing the old structure, drop it. Rollback is possible "at most points". After reads move, new-only data is lost on rollback (https://www.prisma.io/dataguide/types/relational/expand-and-contract-pattern).
- **Stripe's four steps:** dual write, move reads, move writes, remove old data, with consistency checks at each step (https://stripe.com/blog/online-migrations).
- **Down migrations are rarely needed.** Fowler and Sadalage: reverse migrations are rarely worth it. Write migrations that work with both the old and the new schema instead (https://martinfowler.com/articles/evodb.html). Azure: "Rolling back changes, especially database, schema, or other stateful component changes, can be complex" (Azure SDP page).
- **Railway rollback limits that matter for the live site:**
  - rollback restores the old image and variables only while the image is retained: Free 24 h, Hobby 72 h, Pro 120 h, Enterprise 360 h;
  - after that only Redeploy, which rebuilds;
  - rollback does not cover schema or data;
  - "Until `main` is fixed, the next merge redeploys the bad code" (https://railway.com/guides/roll-back-bad-deploy, https://railway.com/guides/ship-on-merge-pr-canaries).
  - The live site may stay on one version for weeks, so its rollback target must be a git ref, not an image. Railway lets a service choose its trigger branch and turn off autodeploy (https://docs.railway.com/deployments/github-autodeploys).
  - Google SRE release practice: cut a release from mainline at a revision, fix bugs on mainline, cherry-pick fixes into the release (https://sre.google/sre-book/release-engineering/).

## 6. A solo, non-developer owner with AI agents: simplicity or isolation?
- **The evidence points to isolating data from agents, not to more environments.**
  - The Replit incident and the fix (an agent cannot modify the production database; it reads through a replica) target the most valuable failure mode (Fortune and Replit docs above).
  - Azure SDP: "There are no low-risk deployments to production"; "Deployments should be performed by computers, not humans" (SRE workbook). Read "humans" there as ad hoc agents: everything goes through the same automated path.
- **Railway access control adds nothing on Hobby or Pro.** Project membership is shared across environments, and per-environment RBAC is Enterprise-only (Railway isolation guide). A second Railway environment would not stop an agent that holds the project token. Database roles and credentials are the separation EDGE can actually enforce.
- **The cost and drift of a full copy fall on the operator.** Here that is the AI agents and the user's budget (Railway drift warning; Railway pricing).

Conclusion: simplicity at the website layer (two edge-bff services) is acceptable. Isolation is needed at the customer-data layer and in the change path.

## 7. Applied to EDGE's architecture: gaps in "one environment, two websites" as planned (EXEC.md:15997-16021)

**Repository facts**
- edge-bff and screener-worker deploy from `main` with check suites on (`.railway/railway.ts` edge-bff about line 246, screener-worker about 231). backtest-worker is uploaded through the CLI (about 214). terminal-api has no GitHub source in the file (about 191).
- The Postgres limit is 2 GB and 1 vCPU (`.railway/railway.ts:20`).
- Postgres restarts are scheduled at 09:45 and 20:45 WIB, about 12 s of downtime each (AGENTS.md). 09:45 falls in IDX trading hours, and 20:45 is evening use, so live users will hit both.
- edge-bff loops:
  - backtest job loop (`apps/edge-bff/README.md:135`);
  - hourly result purge (README:168);
  - hourly session clean-up (README:497);
  - email sender on `edge_bff.email_outbox` (README:792, 851);
  - account seed under an advisory lock (README:798-802).

**Gaps and the fix for each**
1. **The live site must not follow `main`.** Without a pin, a push to `main` updates "live" immediately, which defeats the purpose.
   - Fix: give edge-bff-live a trigger branch `live`. "Push ke live" means fast-forwarding `live` to a commit that is green on the beta. Rollback means moving `live` back and redeploying. This does not depend on the 72/120 h image retention.
   - Record `RAILWAY_GIT_COMMIT_SHA` on both sites, as the canary guide recommends.
2. **The shared back-end changes under live without the beta gate.** terminal-api, the workers and Orc serve both sites as soon as they deploy.
   - Fix: a contract rule that each shared service accepts requests from both the current live version and the beta version.
   - Add a CI test that runs the live commit's client calls against the new service (Azure: "contract stability tests").
   - Allow at most two concurrent website versions (Fowler canary).
3. **Migrations go to the database that will hold paying users' accounts.**
   - Expand-contract only. A contract (drop or rename) runs only after `live` has moved past every reader.
   - Take a backup or snapshot before any `edge_bff` migration. Railway Postgres backup or point-in-time restore capability was NOT researched here and needs checking.
   - Least-privilege database roles: agents' ad hoc and data-job logins get no write or DDL rights on the `edge_bff` schema. Only the migration path, with the user's go, gets them. This mirrors Replit's "agent cannot modify production".
4. **Background loops and side effects.** Give each loop one owner, the live site, or guard it with a Postgres advisory lock. Postgres docs: advisory locks have "application-defined meanings" and session-level locks are held until released or the session ends (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/explicit-locking.html).
   - The beta must not send email to real users.
   - The beta must not run purges written for another code version.
   - The beta must not seed accounts.
   - This follows the Railway guidance to disable outbound side effects in canaries.
5. **One Postgres for heavy jobs and live users.** SRE's shared-backend warning applies: a backfill, rebuild or out-of-memory event on the 2 GB market Postgres takes the live sign-in and accounts down with it. Planned restarts fall in user hours.
   - Fix at launch: move the restart times out of trading and evening hours, with the user's approval.
   - Stage 2: put `edge_bff` (accounts, sessions, subscriptions, outbox, jobs) on its own small Postgres. At $10/GB-month, 0.25-0.5 GB is about $2.5-5/month plus storage. That is an estimate; real usage was not measured.
6. **Admin and beta security.** Different hosts, `__Host-` cookies with no `Domain`, separate session secrets, MFA for admin, admin-only enforced on the server for every beta request, and no admin tools on the live host (NIST SC-2, OWASP).
7. **Parity.** Same image build, same backing-service versions (12-factor). Configuration differs only in variables: site origin, cookie secret, loop ownership, email on or off. Code never branches on environment to pick credentials ("Your application should never branch on environment to pick credentials", Railway isolation guide).

## 8. Proposed path for the user
- **Stage 1, launch (the user's choice, with guardrails).** One Railway environment. edge-bff stays the beta (admin only, Railway address). edge-bff-live is on the domain, deploys from branch `live`, and moves only on "push ke live" with every suite green. Add guardrails 1-7. Extra cost: one small web service, probably $2-5/month (estimate, not measured).
- **Stage 2, when real users or payments exist (or after the first incident).** Move the `edge_bff` schema to its own small Postgres that only edge-bff and edge-bff-live logins can write. Agents get read-only access there, and migrations need the user's go. Market data stays produced once and published through the bucket and terminal-api. This gives "customer data isolated, market data shared read-only" without copying 23 GB or the 26 services.
- **Stage 3, only if the team or compliance grows.** A separate Railway production environment (option 2 in EXEC.md, "light production"). It holds edge-bff-live, terminal-api, the two workers and the account Postgres, and reads the published market files from the dev bucket. Bucket read-only credentials and cross-environment public access need checking first. A full copy (option 1) is not recommended at any stage for this team size.

## 9. Not verified in this research (check before deciding)
- Whether Railway buckets support read-only credentials.
- Railway Postgres backup and point-in-time restore on the current plan.
- Logical replication on Railway Postgres (`wal_level`).
- The current Railway plan (Hobby or Pro, which sets image retention at 72 h or 120 h).
- Memory edge-bff actually uses, for the cost of the second site.
- Indonesian PDP law (UU 27/2022) duties for account data.
- The official OWASP pages were reachable only through mirrors (Developer Guide Administrative Interfaces; ASVS 4.3.1).
- Google's dark-launch article did not load. Fowler's definition was used instead.

No files were changed. No Railway or database calls were made.

The IaC docs add: "A project token is scoped to one environment, so the workflow applies to that environment only." https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code.md
- Deploy branch per environment, and per service:
  - "Each service in each environment has its own deployment trigger". The guide shows staging set to branch `staging` and production to `main`. https://railway.com/guides/isolate-staging-production
  - The trigger branch is set in Service Settings. https://docs.railway.com/guides/github-autodeploys
  - Two services in the same environment can therefore follow different branches. This is my inference from the per-service setting; no doc names that exact case.
  - IaC: `github("owner/repo", { branch: "main" })`, and `ctx.environment` / `ctx.isEnvironment()` render a different desired state per environment. https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code/reference.md
  - The branch can also be set by CLI/API (`source.branch`, changelog 2026-01-23).
  - Config-as-code (railway.json) is deprecated and stops being read on 2026-12-01; railway.ts (IaC, TypeScript GA) replaces it. https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code.md

== 2. NETWORKING ==
- The private network is per environment: "Each environment has its own isolated network"; DNS is `SERVICE.railway.internal`; it works across regions inside one environment. https://docs.railway.com/reference/private-networking
- Railway guide: "Nothing in staging can reach production over the private network ... there is no route between the two networks". Public domains stay reachable from the internet in any environment. https://railway.com/guides/isolate-staging-production
- Staff (brody, 2024-06-03): "The private network is isolated to a single environment in a single project ... They all need to be in the same environment within the same project." https://station.railway.com/questions/connect-to-private-database-url-between-812032e0
- Cross-environment access is only possible over the public network. For Postgres this means enabling Public Access, which creates a TCP Proxy and DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL, and "you will be billed for Network Egress". https://docs.railway.com/guides/postgresql
- "Traffic over the TCP proxy is billed as network egress." https://railway.com/guides/postgres-backups-restores.md
- TCP proxy: you choose the internal port and Railway gives a domain plus port. If Cloudflare is in front, proxying must be off. https://docs.railway.com/reference/tcp-proxy
- Private traffic is free. This is a community/bot answer; I found no official pricing line: "traffic over the private network between services in the same project (*.railway.internal) is free". https://station.railway.com/questions/egress-billing-on-a-private-network-0321e807
- Shared variables are defined per environment (Project Settings > Shared Variables). "Every variable value is scoped to one environment." https://railway.com/guides/isolate-staging-production
- References: `${{shared.X}}`, `${{SERVICE.VAR}}`. The docs give no syntax for referencing another environment, and the community found none (a thread reports `${{Service.VAR}}` failing to resolve in PR envs). https://docs.railway.com/guides/variables ; https://station.railway.com/questions/cross-service-variable-references-se-66a86e71
- An IaC `ctx.shared.NAME` "points at an existing shared variable on the environment; it does not define or manage" it. https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code/reference.md

== 3. DATABASES ==
- Volume backups:
  - Schedules: daily (kept 6 days), weekly (kept 27 days), monthly (kept 89 days); several can be combined; manual backups are also possible.
  - Incremental copy-on-write, billed at the volume rate per GB-minute for unique data only.
  - "Backups can only be restored into the same project + environment." A restore creates a new volume mounted at the same path; the old one is kept unmounted; the change is staged and then redeployed.
  - Manual backups are capped relative to volume size (the page says 50%). Wiping a volume deletes its backups.
  - The page calls the feature newer and still under development.
  - https://docs.railway.com/reference/backups
- PITR:
  - Postgres runs pgBackRest WAL archiving to a Railway bucket, with weekly full and daily differential backups. "The last 4 full backups are retained, giving you a restore window of roughly 4 weeks."
  - A restore creates "a brand-new Postgres service alongside the source", "in the project". The page does NOT say whether that service can be placed in another environment.
  - Cutover is manual. The window starts at the first base backup after enabling, not before.
  - Cost: no separate fee; bucket storage at $0.015/GB-month plus egress on uploads (compressed).
  - Postgres minor-version pinning is not supported with PITR.
  - The page does not state plan availability.
  - https://docs.railway.com/volumes/point-in-time-recovery.md
- Portable copy: a logical dump (`railway connect postgres --tunnel-only`, then pg_dump/pg_restore) restores "Anywhere: another Railway service, another provider, your laptop". This is the only documented route into another environment. https://railway.com/guides/postgres-backups-restores.md
- Users report that a local dump through the tunnel is slow (about 10 MB in 10 minutes). There was no staff answer; community workarounds were a temporary service with rsync/cp, or a backup restore (same environment only). https://station.railway.com/questions/fastest-way-to-clone-my-production-postg-1cc96fc6
- HA: Railway Postgres "can be converted into a high-availability cluster with automatic failover" (Patroni, etcd and HAProxy). https://docs.railway.com/guides/postgresql
- Read replicas: available only as marketplace templates, not a native feature:
  - Postgres HA Read Replica (pg_auto_failover, 3 services): https://railway.com/deploy/postgres-ha-read-replica
  - Postgres Read Replicas (Patroni, reads on port 5433): https://railway.com/deploy/postgres-read-replicas--deploy-postgres-read-replicas
- Logical replication: no Railway doc. A pg_easy_replicate template exists. A source would need wal_level=logical, which the docs do not cover for the Railway image.
- Replication across environments would have to go over the TCP proxy, which means public egress at $0.05/GB.
- Cost of any replica or extra Postgres: a full container (memory, CPU and volume at the rates in section 5). Railway publishes no per-feature price.

== 4. BUCKETS ==
- Per environment, each with its own credentials (S3-compatible, in the Credentials tab). "Buckets are currently only accessible via public networking." https://docs.railway.com/guides/storage-buckets
- The docs do not say whether another environment may use a bucket. Because access is public S3 with credentials, a service in any environment (or outside Railway) holding the credentials can technically read or write it. That is my inference, not a documented guarantee.
- Copy Objects is a supported S3 operation. The region cannot be changed after creation: to move, create a new bucket, copy and repoint. https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code/reference.md
- Price: $0.015/GB-month, counted across all of the workspace's buckets, averaged daily and rounded up to the next whole GB-month. "All S3 API operations are unlimited and free"; bucket egress is free, but uploads from services count as service egress. Hobby is capped at 1 TB total; Pro is unlimited. https://docs.railway.com/storage-buckets/billing.md

== 5. PRICES (railway.com/pricing and docs.railway.com/reference/pricing, read 2026-11-19) ==
- Memory: $10/GB-month ($0.00000386/GB-s; $0.000231/GB-min).
- vCPU: $20/vCPU-month ($0.00000772/vCPU-s).
- Volume: $0.15/GB-month.
- Egress: $0.05/GB.
- Bucket: $0.015/GB-month, operations free.
- Builds: free.
- Sources: https://railway.com/pricing ; https://docs.railway.com/reference/pricing
- Plans:
  - Free: $0, includes $1/month.
  - Hobby: $5/month, includes $5.
  - Pro: $20/month per workspace, includes $20, seats unlimited.
  - Included usage does not carry over, and the subscription is a minimum charge. https://docs.railway.com/reference/pricing/plans
- Hobby vs Pro:
  - Per service: 48 vCPU / 48 GB vs 1,000 vCPU / 1 TB.
  - Replicas: 6 vs 42.
  - Logs: 7 vs 30 days.
  - Services: 50 vs 100.
  - Volume: 5 GB vs 1 TB.
  - Custom domains per service: 2 vs 20.
  - Concurrent builds: 3 vs 10.
  - Image retention after a deployment is removed: Hobby 72 h, Pro 120 h, Enterprise 360 h, Free/Trial 24 h.
- Memory billing and page cache: the pricing page says only VM/sandbox billing includes the "filesystem cache". It does not say the same for containers. The repo's own measurements (railway.ts comments) show that container page cache is billed in practice.
- Idle small service: Railway publishes no number. It bills usage only, roughly $1 per 0.1 GB held all month plus CPU (repo measurement: edge-bff about USD 1.00/month).
- Serverless (sleepApplication): the service sleeps 5-10 minutes after its last outbound packet. Private-network traffic and open DB connections keep it awake. The first request may return 502. "Slept services still consume a slot". The docs do not state billing while asleep. https://docs.railway.com/reference/app-sleeping

== 6. DOMAINS ==
- Limits: Hobby 2 custom domains per service; Pro 20 per service by default, raisable on request. Trial allows 1 (apex and www count as 2).
- Several domains on one service are allowed, each with its own target port.
- Wildcards are supported but not nested; they need a TXT record plus an _acme-challenge CNAME.
- DNS: a CNAME plus a verification TXT, both required (without the TXT the domain returns 404). Propagation can take up to 72 h.
- Apex domains need CNAME flattening or ALIAS (Cloudflare, yes; Route 53, Azure DNS and GoDaddy, no).
- Cloudflare proxied: SSL must be "Full"; "Full (Strict) will not work as intended".
- TLS: Let's Encrypt ECDSA, "should happen within an hour", 90-day certificates renewed with 30 days left.
- Source for the above: https://docs.railway.com/networking/domains/working-with-domains.md
- IaC can declare `domains: ["app.example.com"]` per service; generated *.up.railway.app domains are not managed in railway.ts. https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code/reference.md
- Moving a domain between services or environments: the docs do NOT cover it. Staff procedure (brody, 2025-01-26):
  1. Remove the domain from the old service but keep the CNAME.
  2. Add it to the new service.
  3. Wait for the certificate (ignore "incorrect value").
  4. Then update the DNS.
  - This gives "minimal downtime". A domain sits on one service at a time.
  - Users report stuck "Not available" reservations that only support could release.
  - https://station.railway.com/questions/migrate-custom-domain-from-a-service-to-c35d5b86 ; https://station.railway.com/questions/custom-domain-stuck-on-stale-railway-ser-ebc4e4db

== 7. DEPLOY CONTROLS ==
- Wait for CI (IaC `checkSuites`):
  - "new deployments sit in a WAITING state until every GitHub Actions check suite on the commit has finished". A failure skips the deploy; still running after 2 h also skips it.
  - Checks from other GitHub apps are ignored. It requires workflows with an `on: push` trigger (pull_request/workflow_dispatch cannot gate).
  - Sources: https://docs.railway.com/guides/github-autodeploys ; https://station.railway.com/questions/pre-deployment-confirmation-rollback-w-b07a3598 (Railway, 2026-11-12)
- Manual approval: no deploy-approval gate is documented. The options are:
  - disable auto-deploys and deploy manually ("Deploy Latest Commit" in Cmd+K, which deploys the latest commit of the connected branch);
  - staged changes, which apply only to config changes;
  - in IaC GitHub Actions, "Merging is the approval".
  - Sources: https://docs.railway.com/guides/github-autodeploys ; https://docs.railway.com/infrastructure-as-code.md
- Rollback:
  - From the three-dot menu of an older deployment. It restores that deployment's image and custom variables with no rebuild ("completes in seconds").
  - It works only within the image retention after the deployment was removed (Pro 120 h); after that, Redeploy rebuilds from the original source and variables.
  - The docs do not mention volume data or DB migrations.
  - Volume-backed services cannot run two deployments at once, so each deploy has brief downtime.
  - Sources: https://railway.com/guides/roll-back-bad-deploy.md ; https://docs.railway.com/guides/deployment-actions ; https://docs.railway.com/reference/pricing/plans
- Pinning to a commit:
  - The dashboard has no arbitrary-commit picker. "Currently, there is no way to force a deploy from a branch other than the Default" without changing the service's trigger branch. https://docs.railway.com/guides/deployment-actions
  - Community: the GraphQL `serviceInstanceDeployV2` accepts `commitSha`, validated against the connected repo, and a persistent `source.commitSha` pin exists. Not in the official docs. https://station.railway.com/questions/supported-first-exact-sha-deployment-wit-14751110 ; https://station.railway.com/community/how-to-remove-source-commitsha-pin-witho-855ac31e
  - Image sources can be pinned by tag (`image("ghcr.io/x:1.2.3")`, autoUpdates disabled/patch/minor). Digest pinning is not documented.
- Pre-deploy command (for example migrations) is supported (`preDeploy` in railway.ts).

== IMPLICATIONS FOR THE CHOSEN DESIGN (my inference, for the proposal) ==
1. Railway's own isolation guide puts the production boundary at a separate environment. That gives:
   - a separate private network;
   - separate secrets (sealed variables not copied);
   - a separate bucket;
   - a project token scoped to that environment. This last point is the only Pro-plan hard boundary that keeps AI agents (who hold a dev-scoped token) out of production. Environment RBAC needs Enterprise.
2. A separate environment cannot use dev's Postgres or services privately. The options would be:
   - the TCP proxy: public exposure plus $0.05/GB egress and latency;
   - its own Postgres plus a copy. Backups restore only into the same environment, volume copy is PR-only beta, so the copy would be a logical dump or replication over the public proxy;
   - published files written to the production bucket, which any environment holding the credentials can reach over public S3.
   This is why a full or light production environment costs data-pipeline work, and why "one environment, two web services" is a viable pragmatic pattern (a beta/live release channel on the web tier) that Railway supports: each service has its own trigger branch.
3. Supported mechanics for edge-bff-live in `dev`:
   - trigger branch `live` (railway.ts `github(..., { branch: "live", checkSuites: true })`);
   - "push ke live" = fast-forward `live` to a commit whose checks are green. Wait for CI needs the workflows to run on push to `live` too.
   - rollback = previous deployment within 120 h, else redeploy;
   - custom domain on edge-bff-live (Pro: 20 per service; Cloudflare SSL "Full", not Strict);
   - idle cost about USD 1/month (repo measurement for edge-bff).
4. Gaps vs best practice in the chosen design:
   - Shared services (terminal-api, backtest-worker, screener-worker, orc, data jobs) still deploy from `main` straight to live users. Only edge-bff and screener-worker are CI-gated today.
   - DB migrations hit live at once, so they must be expand/contract.
   - The agents' credentials cover live.
   - There is no Railway-level separation of secrets or logs.
   - Cheap mitigations: live copies of the small stateless user-facing services that also follow `live` (measured idle about USD 0.5-1.5/month each); Wait for CI on every shared service; a dev-scoped project token for agents if a production environment is ever created.
